content: Dextromethorphan, commonly referred to by its street names such as CCC, DXM, Orange Crush, Red Devils, Robo, Robo-trippin, Skittles, Triple C, and Tussin, is an antitussive medication primarily used to suppress cough. It is a common ingredient in many over-the-counter cold and cough remedies. Beyond its role as a cough suppressant, dextromethorphan has been explored for other medical applications, including pain relief and psychological treatments. In its pure form, dextromethorphan appears as a white crystalline powder. However, it is typically administered in the form of syrups, tablets, or lozenges, available under various brand names and generic labels. When consumed at doses exceeding the medically recommended range, dextromethorphan acts as a dissociative hallucinogen, producing neurotoxic and hallucinogenic effects similar to those of ketamine and phencyclidine (PCP). This property makes it susceptible to abuse. Chemistry Dextromethorphan hydrobromide monohydrate is a salt derived from the methyl ether dextrorotatory isomer of levorphanol, a narcotic analgesic. Its chemical name is 3-methoxy-17-methyl-9(alpha), 13(alpha), 14(alpha)-morphinan hydrobromide monohydrate. It appears as white crystals, is sparingly soluble in water, and freely soluble in alcohol. Indications The primary indication for dextromethorphan is as a cough suppressant, providing temporary relief from coughs caused by minor throat and bronchial irritation, such as those associated with the common cold or exposure to inhaled irritants. Additionally, a combination of dextromethorphan and quinidine has been shown to alleviate symptoms of pseudobulbar affect, characterized by inappropriate episodes of laughing or crying, in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and multiple sclerosis (MS). Dextromethorphan is also being investigated as a potential treatment for fibromyalgia-related pain and as an aid in breaking addictions to narcotics and other habit-forming substances, including nicotine. For addiction treatment, its efficacy is enhanced when combined with an oxidase inhibitor like quinidine. Pharmacokinetics At therapeutic doses, dextromethorphan acts centrally to elevate the cough threshold without impairing ciliary activity. It is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with effects beginning within 15–60 minutes of ingestion. The duration of action is approximately 3–8 hours for dextromethorphan hydrobromide and 10–12 hours for the extended-release form, dextromethorphan polistirex. However, its use in atopic children is limited due to the potential for histamine release, which can trigger allergic reactions. The typical antitussive dose ranges from 10 mg to 30 mg, with the re-dosing interval depending on the specific preparation. Side Effects Dextromethorphan use can result in side effects such as body rash or itching, dissociation, nausea, gastrointestinal disturbances, drowsiness, dizziness, excitement, vomiting, blurred vision, dilated pupils, sweating, fever, hypertension, shallow respiration, diarrhea, urinary retention, and increased heart rate, blood pressure, and body temperature. Psychological dependence may develop due to its recreational use potential, although it does not cause physical addiction, as noted by the WHO Committee on Drug Dependence. When combined with guaifenesin, an expectorant, high doses are more likely to cause nausea and vomiting. Olney's Lesions High doses of dextromethorphan, like other NMDA receptor antagonists, are hypothesized to cause a type of brain damage known as Olney's lesions. Studies in rats have shown that high doses of NMDA receptor antagonists, such as MK-801, can lead to vacuole formation in certain brain regions, which may develop into irreversible lesions. However, it is important to note that injected dextromethorphan has been associated with vacuolization in rats, whereas oral administration does not appear to produce the same effect. Drug Interactions Dextromethorphan should not be taken with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), or central nervous system (CNS) depressants such as alcohol, antihistamines, and psychotropics, as these combinations can lead to cumulative CNS depressant effects. CYP2D6 inhibitors, including medications like fluoxetine, paroxetine, and quinidine, can increase the effects of dextromethorphan, potentially leading to serotonin syndrome, a life-threatening condition caused by excessive serotonergic activity. Contraindications Dextromethorphan should be administered to atopic children only under strict medical supervision. Clinical Pharmacology After oral administration, dextromethorphan is rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, enters the bloodstream, and crosses the blood-brain barrier. During first-pass metabolism in the liver, it is converted into an active metabolite, dextrorphan, which contributes to its therapeutic effects. Dextromethorphan is metabolized by liver enzymes, undergoing O-demethylation (producing dextrorphan), N-demethylation, and partial conjugation with glucuronic acid and sulfate ions. The metabolites, along with trace amounts of the unchanged drug, are detectable in urine hours after administration. The primary metabolic pathway involves the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2D6. Individuals with a functional deficiency in this enzyme, known as poor CYP2D6 metabolizers, may experience prolonged effects and action of dextromethorphan. Recreational Use Dextromethorphan has been misused as a recreational drug to induce intoxication. At doses 7 to 50 times the therapeutic range, it can alter consciousness, with effects ranging from euphoria to hallucinations and out-of-body experiences. Chronic high-dose use can lead to toxic psychosis and other permanent psychological issues. Recreational use often involves slang terms like tussin, robo, dex, and skittles. Due to concerns about abuse, many retailers in the U.S. have restricted access to dextromethorphan-containing products, requiring customers to request them from a pharmacist or meet age restrictions. Classification At high doses, dextromethorphan is classified as a dissociative hallucinogen, similar to ketamine and PCP. While it does not typically produce withdrawal symptoms associated with physical addiction, cases of psychological addiction have been reported. Legality Dextromethorphan-containing antitussive preparations are legal for purchase in most pharmacies worldwide. However, its sale in pure powder form may incur penalties in the U.S. due to incidental violations of related drug laws. Dextromethorphan is excluded from the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) of 1970 but could be added if recreational use increases. Effects At low recreational doses (under 200 mg), dextromethorphan produces euphoria. Higher doses (around 400 mg) may cause intense euphoria or dysphoria, vivid imagination, and closed-eye hallucinations. Very high doses (600 mg and above) can result in profound alterations in consciousness, out-of-body experiences, or temporary psychosis. Frequent high-dose use can lead to toxic psychosis and other permanent psychological problems. Most users find such high doses uncomfortable and avoid repeating them. Duration The effects of recreational dosing generally last as long as the medical dosing of the same preparation. Extended-release forms, such as dextromethorphan-polistirex, produce longer-lasting effects than shorter-acting forms like dextromethorphan-hydrobromide. Dosage has little impact on the duration of effects but may intensify them. An afterglow effect may persist for 1 to 14 hours after the primary effects wear off. Psychopharmacology The psychological effects of dextromethorphan are largely attributed to its metabolite, dextrorphan (DXO), which is a more potent NMDA receptor antagonist than dextromethorphan itself. Both DXM and DXO inhibit neurotransmitters like glutamate from activating receptors in the brain, leading to dissociation and a sense of disconnection. The euphoric effects of DXM may be linked to increased dopamine levels, although this is a disputed subject. Chronic high-dose use can result in toxic psychosis or other psychological issues. Additionally, overdosing on accompanying active ingredients in multi-symptom cold medications can cause permanent physiological damage.
